name: Kira Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I deliver around our harbour town and the caravan parks along the coast, mostly groceries and meal kits through two apps, and parcels on quiet days. I've got a little white van I bought outright last spring. Summer is crazy with the holiday lets, winter is slow, and I'm still learning the back lanes, eleven months in. I like it because it feels like my own small business, even if the apps pretend they're the boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you run it like a business?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. A chatbot keeps my mileage log, works out my tax, and tells me which app pays better on which day. I'm engaged to Tom, who crews on a fishing boat, and we're getting married in the chapel on the cliff next year. I've got about a year of money saved, and my gran left me a share of her cottage, so I'm not worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to building things the normal way. I'd say it in the town's business group on my phone. Hard work and small firms are what keep a town alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can grow my own little round. I'd love to start my own courier firm for the town's shops, without the apps in the middle. With savings and a van, I could do it in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the apps for now, but start doing direct deliveries for the bakery and the fishmonger who've asked me. Use AI to build a simple booking page and invoices. Save as normal for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient to get going on my own. I've been planning it in my head for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd be disappointed about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I was hoping AI would make running a small firm cheaper. If it stalls, I'll still use what's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on the work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winter. Holiday lets go quiet and the apps send hardly anything. The shops are open all year, so I want my own customers instead of waiting on holiday lets and the apps.

I'd post in the town's **business group** about building things the normal way.
think: I can **grow my own round** and cut out the apps.
With **savings and a van**, I could start my own firm within two years.
do: Start **direct deliveries** for the bakery and fishmonger.
Use AI to build a **booking page** and invoices.
Keep **saving** for the wedding as normal.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **impatient** to go out on her own.
S0.quote: The shops are open all year, so I want my own customers instead of waiting on holiday lets and the apps.
fieldNote: Sees herself as a **small business owner**, not a gig worker.
Uses AI **daily** for tax and planning, despite a traditional outlook.
Faith and **marriage** plans sit alongside ambition.
**Winter slack** is her real pressure.

steps.text: Start direct deliveries for the harbour bakery and fishmonger
Build a booking page and invoices with a chatbot
Keep saving for next year's chapel wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for anyone willing to work. The government should get out of the way and let small firms try things. I'd post about it in the business group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's great for me. The booking, invoicing and customer messages are exactly the bits I hate. If AI does the booking and invoicing, I'm a one-woman firm that runs like a bigger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my own delivery service for the town's shops this year. AI handles the booking and texts, I do the driving. I'd still do the apps in the slow months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even. I'd be up late making plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes over booking, buying and answering customers. Does that help or hurt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helps. The bits that slow down a small firm are the thinking bits. The driving is still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fishing is hands-on and weather-dependent, so it's safe for now. His skipper might use AI to plan trips, but someone still has to haul the nets.

think: AI does exactly the **booking and invoicing** I hate.
I become a **one-woman firm** that runs like a bigger one.
do: **Launch** her own delivery service for the town's shops this year.
Let **AI handle bookings** and texts while she drives.
Keep **the apps** for the slow months.
S1.quote: If AI does the booking and invoicing, I'm a one-woman firm that runs like a bigger one.
fieldNote: She sees the thinking-task wave as a **gift** to small firms.
**Free-market** view: government should step back.
Tom's fishing feels **safe** to her.
Very clear on which parts are **thinking** and which are hands-on.

steps.text: Launch a delivery service for the harbour town's shops
Let AI take bookings and send customer texts
Keep the grocery apps running through the winter months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but the people who move fast will be fine. I'd tell the business group to plan now. I'd say families and towns need to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my driving goes by 2031, but my firm doesn't have to. If I own the customers, I can buy a robot van when the robots arrive. The worry is whether big firms undercut me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the courier firm hard in the next two years and lock the shops into contracts. Save for a robot van, or join with two other local drivers to buy one. Use AI to watch prices and learn what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly. It's a race, and I don't know yet who else is running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work by 2031. What happens to your own firm then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about whether to wait on kids. Probably we'd still marry, but we'd hold off on a baby for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fishing might change too, if robots can work boats. We'd want one steady income, and right now that's harder to see.

say: I'd say people who **move fast** will be fine.
I'd tell the business group to **plan now** and stick together.
think: My **driving goes** by 2031, but my firm doesn't have to.
The worry is **big firms** undercutting me first.
do: Lock the town's shops into **contracts** over the next two years.
Save for a **robot van**, maybe with two other drivers.
Use AI to **watch prices** and what's coming.
S2.quote: If I own the customers, I can buy a robot van when the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Plans to **own robots**, not compete with them.
Fears **big firms** more than the robots themselves.
Might **delay a baby**, a real family change.
**Adaptive** and secure enough to stay uneasy, not anxious.

steps.text: Sign the harbour shops to delivery contracts
Buy a robot delivery van with two local drivers
Hold off on starting a family for a year or two
Use AI to track prices and robot van releases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, and small firms should get ahead. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. I'd have six or seven years to build the firm before robots. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the firm slowly, add a second van in 2029, maybe hire a part-timer. Use AI for everything that's paperwork. Save to buy robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like having a clear road ahead with the tank full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, one or two locals, maybe my cousin. But I'd be honest with them that the robots are coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me grow first and automate later, and with two years I'd be rushing. Rushing is how small firms go bust.

say: I'd say there's **time** to do this **properly**.
I'd tell young people to **learn a trade** and start something.
think: I'd have **six or seven years** to build the firm.
That's **plenty** of time for me to build customers before buying robots.
do: Add a **second van** in 2029 and maybe hire a part-timer.
S3.quote: Five years lets me grow first and automate later, and with two years I'd be rushing.
fieldNote: The extra time makes her **plan comfortable**.
Would **hire locals** but be honest about robots.
Balances **growth now** with automation later.
Strong savings and **adaptability** keep her calm.

steps.text: Buy a second delivery van in 2029
Use AI for invoices, bookings and tax
Save towards buying delivery robots around 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who works hard can be ready. I'd keep posting in the business group about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's perfect. I'd have a firm, a family and time to switch to robots when it suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow the firm, marry Tom, have kids in a few years. Buy robots when they're proven and cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and hopeful. It feels like a fair start for my generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to robots in 2039. How does that land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, getting comfortable. I'd check every year whether things are speeding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in having so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-nine, with a firm that runs robots and employs a few people. That's the dream.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** for anyone who works hard.
I'd keep **posting** about it in the business group.
think: It's **perfect** for me: time to build a firm and start a family.
I'd **switch to robots** when it suits me.
do: Buy robots when they're **proven and cheap**.
S4.quote: I'd be thirty-nine, with a firm that runs robots and employs a few people.
fieldNote: The long timeline fits her **business plans**.
Family plans, **marriage and kids**, go ahead.
Watches for **complacency** with a yearly check.
Sees robots as **tools she'll own**.

steps.text: Grow the harbour courier firm to several vans
Marry Tom and plan for children
Buy delivery robots once they're proven and cheap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because big firms with robots could crush small ones before we're ready. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy robots, and rules that stop big firms undercutting locals.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small business. Everyone talks about workers or big companies, but people like me are in the middle.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about workers or big companies, but people like me are in the middle.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** driver in a harbour town who runs her round like a business.
She uses **AI daily** for tax, planning and bookings.
She has a **year saved**, a share of a cottage and marries Tom next year.
She's **traditional** on family and markets but eager to own robots.
She stays **calm** in most pictures, uneasy only when robots come by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big firms with robots could crush small ones first.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small firms to buy robots.
